To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) MIP is a risk factor for first infection in infants in southern Benin; 2) the effect of MIF on first infection in infants is modified by local transmission; 3) this effect is best estimated using an exposure prediction model based on local climatic, ecological, and behavioral factors; and 4) the use of such a prediction model improves the goodness of fit and allows the effect of Mif to be estimated with greater accuracy.

the risk of first malaria infection in infancy is increased in infants born to women with a malaria-infected (as opposed to malaria-negative) placenta, and that this increased risk is not attributable to the local malaria transmission.

the effect of Malaria-Infected Placenta on the risk of first malaria infection in children was not significant in a model adjusted for "village-like variables" (i.e., variables not taking into account local transmission) but became significant in a model using spatiotemporeal transmission prediction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of the placental infection in malaria on the first malaria infection in the infant.
the importance of adequate spatiotemporally local transmission measures in malaria cohorts.
the effect of malaria-infected placental infection on time to first infection in infants.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the risk of a first infection in infants whose mother was infected at delivery is not significantly increased, but this statement must be qualified by the fact that the effect of the MIP was not demonstrated because the effect of local malaria transmission was not taken into account.
the risk of a first infection is increased in infants whose mother had a MIP, and that this effect is not explained by the local spatiotemporally varying malaria transmission.

the risk of malaria infection in infants is higher when their mothers have a malaria-infected-placenta and that this risk is further increased when the infants are born in a high-transmission context.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, to study the relation between placenta malaria and first malaria in infants, we should take into account the local spatiotemporally variable malaria transmission.
malaria transmission is an important determinant of the effect of placenta infection on first infant malaria.
the effect of placenta malaria on the risk of malaria infection in infants should be assessed in relation to local malaria transmission.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, to demonstrate the immune-tolerance hypothesis in the relation between MIP and first malaria infection, the effect of MIF should be assessed by adjusting for local spatiotemporally varying malaria transmission measures.

the use of exposure variables based on climatic, environmental and behavioral factors can help to better understand the effect of a biological variable on malaria infection, and to better estimate its effect.
, when studying the impact of a risk factor on a health outcome, it is essential to take into account the spatiotemporo-exposure to malaria.
